source_refs.note: Chapter 26 exercise (PDF 157-159) solved: 10 MCQs keyed from the chapter (no key printed), 10 short (structures as condensed formulas), 2 constructed response and 3 descriptive questions with comparison tables. Book corrections: MCQ II(b), Q2(d).

blocks.prompt: I. Which pair of monomers reacts to form a polyester?
blocks.explanation: A polyester has ester links –COO–; the –OH of a diol reacts with the –COOH of a dicarboxylic acid, removing water (26.1.2). A diamine with a dicarboxylic acid gives a polyamide.

blocks.prompt: II. What small molecule is eliminated when a diamine reacts with a dioyl chloride?
blocks.explanation:
The –NH₂ of the diamine reacts with the –COCl of the dioyl chloride; H from N and Cl from C leave as HCl (26.1.2):
n H₂N–R–NH₂ + n ClOC–R'–COCl → [–HN–R–NH–CO–R'–CO–]ₙ + 2n HCl

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: Option (b) prints the formula as 'Hcl'; hydrogen chloride is HCl (capital C, small l).

blocks.prompt: III. How do plasticizers affect PVC?

options.text: Reduce inter-chain forces, make it flexible

blocks.explanation: Plasticizers reduce the strong forces between the polymer chains, so the chains move more freely and PVC becomes soft and flexible (26.1.1).

blocks.prompt: IV. What are the two monomers for Nylon 6,6?
blocks.explanation: Nylon 6,6 uses hexamethylenediamine H₂N–(CH₂)₆–NH₂ and adipic acid HOOC–(CH₂)₄–COOH; each has six carbon atoms (26.1.2, 26.2).

blocks.prompt: V. A polymer section is shown: [-CH₂-CH(CH₃)-CH₂-CH(CH₃)-]... What is the monomer, and what type of polymer is it?
blocks.explanation: The backbone has only C–C bonds, so it is an addition polymer. The repeat unit is –CH₂–CH(CH₃)–; turning its C–C back into C=C gives CH₂=CH–CH₃, propene (26.3).

blocks.prompt: VI. Polyesters and polyamides are considered biodegradable because they:
blocks.explanation: Soil organisms can attack the ester and amide links by hydrolysis, breaking the polymer into carboxylic acids and alcohols or amines (26.5.1).

blocks.prompt: VII. What are the products of alkaline hydrolysis (saponification) of a polyester?
blocks.explanation:
Hydrolysis of an ester link gives an acid and an alcohol (26.5.1); in alkali (e.g. NaOH) the acid is at once neutralised to its salt:
–CO–O– + NaOH → –COO⁻Na⁺ + HO– (carboxylate salt + alcohol; the alkali step is beyond the chapter)

blocks.prompt: VIII. What are the products of acidic hydrolysis of a polyamide?
blocks.explanation:
Hydrolysis of an amide link gives a carboxylic acid and an amine (26.5.1); in acid the basic amine takes H⁺ and becomes the protonated amine (beyond the chapter):
–CO–NH– + H₂O + H⁺ → –COOH + ⁺H₃N–

blocks.prompt: IX. What is the primary cause of photodegradation in polymers?
blocks.explanation: Groups such as C=O absorb UV light from sunlight; this weakens the bonds in the chain, so the polymer breaks down (26.5.2).

blocks.prompt: X. Poly(alkenes) are considered "chemically inert" because they:

options.text: have strong C-C and C-H bonds.

blocks.explanation: Poly(alkenes) contain only strong, non-polar C–C and C–H bonds with no reactive functional group, so acids, alkalis and microorganisms hardly attack them (26.5).

blocks.prompt:
a) Kevlar® is a thermally and mechanically very stable but flexible polymer; a section of this polymer is given below:
[–C(=O)–C₆H₄–C(=O)–NH–C₆H₄–NH–]ₙ (benzene rings joined at opposite, 1,4-positions)
i) Name the characteristic linkage and type of polymerisation in its structure
ii) Identify the two functional groups that react to form it.
iii) Name the monomers from which it is formed.
blocks.explanation:
i) Amide linkage –CO–NH–; condensation polymerisation (Kevlar is an aromatic polyamide).
ii) The amino group –NH₂ and the carboxylic acid group –COOH (or the acyl chloride group –COCl).
iii) Benzene-1,4-diamine H₂N–C₆H₄–NH₂ and benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid HOOC–C₆H₄–COOH (or benzene-1,4-dicarbonyl chloride ClOC–C₆H₄–COCl) (26.3).

blocks.prompt: b) Explain why the reaction between an acyl chloride and ammonia is classified as a condensation reaction. Identify the small molecule that is eliminated during this reaction.
blocks.explanation:
Two molecules join to form a larger molecule (an amide) and, at the same time, a small molecule is removed; that is a condensation reaction (26.1.2).
CH₃COCl + NH₃ → CH₃CONH₂ + HCl
The small molecule eliminated is hydrogen chloride, HCl.

blocks.prompt:
c) For the following monomers:
ethanedioyl chloride (ClOC–COCl) and ethane-1,2-diol (HO–CH₂–CH₂–OH)
I) Predict the type of the polymer formed.
ii) Draw the repeat unit and a section of the expected polymer.
iii) Name this polymer systematically.
blocks.explanation:
I) Condensation polymer: a polyester (–COCl + –OH give ester links and HCl is eliminated) (26.4.2).
ii) Repeat unit: [–O–CH₂–CH₂–O–CO–CO–]ₙ
Section: …–O–CH₂–CH₂–O–CO–CO–O–CH₂–CH₂–O–CO–CO–…
n ClOC–COCl + n HOCH₂CH₂OH → [–O–CH₂CH₂–O–CO–CO–]ₙ + 2n HCl
iii) Poly(ethane-1,2-diyl ethanedioate), named like poly(ethane-1,2-diyl benzene-1,4-dicarboxylate) (PET).

blocks.prompt:
d) For Nylon 6,6 (from 1,6-hexanediamine and 1,4-hexandioic acid acid):
i) Name the linkage.
ii) Name the small molecule eliminated.
iii) Draw the repeating unit.
blocks.explanation:
i) Amide linkage, –CO–NH–.
ii) Water, H₂O.
iii) [–NH–(CH₂)₆–NH–CO–(CH₂)₄–CO–]ₙ
n H₂N(CH₂)₆NH₂ + n HOOC(CH₂)₄COOH → [–NH(CH₂)₆NH–CO(CH₂)₄CO–]ₙ + 2n H₂O

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The acid is printed '1,4-hexandioic acid acid'. Adipic acid, HOOC–(CH₂)₄–COOH, has its COOH carbons at C1 and C6, so it is hexanedioic acid (hexane-1,6-dioic acid); the word 'acid' is also printed twice.

blocks.prompt:
e) For poly(chloroethene) (PVC)
i) Name the monomer for PVC
ii) Why can it undergo addition polymerization?
blocks.explanation:
i) Chloroethene (vinyl chloride), CH₂=CHCl.
ii) It has a C=C double bond, which opens up so that the monomers add to each other end to end, with nothing lost: n CH₂=CHCl → [–CH₂–CHCl–]ₙ (26.1.1).

blocks.prompt: f) State two properties of nylon that make it suitable for ropes and fishing nets.
blocks.explanation:
1. High tensile strength: strong and resistant to breaking, rubbing and wear.
2. Stretchable (elastic) and resistant to water wear (26.2.1, 26.2.2).

blocks.prompt: g) Give two industrial applications for PVC and two for Nylon.
blocks.explanation:
PVC: (1) pipes and fittings for water supply, drainage and sewage; (2) electrical insulation of wires and cables (26.1.1).
Nylon: (1) automotive parts such as gears, bearings and fuel lines; (2) machine parts such as screws, nuts and bolts (26.2.2).

blocks.prompt: h) Draw the repeating unit of the polyester from propan-1,3-diol and benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid.
blocks.explanation:
HO–CH₂CH₂CH₂–OH + HOOC–C₆H₄–COOH join through ester links with loss of water:
Repeating unit: [–O–CH₂–CH₂–CH₂–O–CO–C₆H₄–CO–]ₙ (C₆H₄ joined at 1,4-positions)

blocks.prompt: i) State three distinct environmental problems caused by the disposal of non-degradable polymers.
blocks.explanation:
1. They persist for a very long time and accumulate in landfills, oceans and landscapes, and they take up huge landfill space.
2. Animals, especially marine life, mistake plastic for food or get tangled, causing choking, injury or starvation.
3. They break into microplastics that pollute soil, water and air and enter the food chain (26.5).

blocks.prompt: j) Name two different polymers used in artificial organs and state the specific application for each.
blocks.explanation:
1. Poly(tetrafluoroethylene) (PTFE): artificial blood vessels (grafts); its smooth surface prevents blood clots.
2. Ultra-high molecular weight polyethylene (UHMWPE): artificial hip and knee joints; smooth, low-friction and wear-resistant (Table 26.2).

blocks.prompt: a) Describe the chemical role of plasticizers in polyvinyl chloride (PVC) and explain how this modification influences the polymer's industrial applications.
blocks.explanation:
Role: plasticizers are chemicals added to PVC that get in between the polymer chains and reduce the strong forces between them. The chains can then slide past each other, so the PVC becomes soft, flexible and easy to shape (26.1.1).
Effect on applications:
• Rigid PVC (no plasticizer): hard, stiff, chemically inert, good insulator, fire resistant, weather resistant; used for pipes and fittings, window frames and door profiles.
• Plasticised PVC: flexible and soft, keeps good chemical and electrical properties but is less rigid; used for insulation of wires and cables, tubing, blood bags and catheters, cling films, raincoats, artificial leather, inflatable products and floor sheets.
So by changing the amount of plasticizer, one polymer is made suitable for both rigid and flexible products.

blocks.prompt: b) Explain why poly(alkenes) like poly(ethene) pose a greater environmental challenge than polyesters and polyamides. Identify the chemical process that allows the latter to degrade.
blocks.explanation:
Poly(alkenes) such as poly(ethene) have a backbone of only strong, non-polar C–C and C–H bonds and no functional group. Water, acids, alkalis and soil microorganisms cannot attack them, so they are non-biodegradable; they persist for very long, fill landfills, harm animals and break into microplastics (26.5).
Polyesters and polyamides contain polar ester (–COO–) and amide (–CONH–) links. Soil organisms can break these links, so the polymers degrade into simpler compounds:
polyester → carboxylic acids + alcohols; polyamide → carboxylic acids + amines (26.5.1).
The chemical process that allows the latter to degrade is hydrolysis of the ester and amide links.

blocks.prompt: Q.4 Compare and contrast addition and condensation polymerization, giving details of the specific structural requirements for the monomers in each.
blocks.explanation:
Similarity: both join a very large number of monomers into long-chain polymers (26.1). The differences, and the structural requirement of the monomers in each, are in the table.
Addition: n CH₂=CH₂ → (initiator, heat/pressure) [–CH₂–CH₂–]ₙ
Condensation: n H₂N–R–NH₂ + n HOOC–R'–COOH → [–HN–R–NH–CO–R'–CO–]ₙ + 2n H₂O

e.g. poly(ethene), PVC, poly(propene)
e.g. nylon 6,6, Kevlar, PET (Terylene)

blocks.prompt: Q.5 Illustrate the formation of two major condensation polymers.
blocks.explanation:
1. Polyester: PET (Terylene) from ethane-1,2-diol and benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid. The –OH of the diol reacts with the –COOH of the acid, forming ester links –CO–O– and removing water (26.1.2):
n HO–CH₂–CH₂–OH + n HOOC–C₆H₄–COOH → [–O–CH₂–CH₂–O–CO–C₆H₄–CO–]ₙ + 2n H₂O
Uses: fibres (an alternative to cotton, crease resistant) and plastic bottles for drinks and food packaging.
2. Polyamide: nylon 6,6 from hexane-1,6-diamine and hexanedioic (adipic) acid. The –NH₂ of the diamine reacts with the –COOH of the acid, forming amide links –CO–NH– and removing water (26.2):
n H₂N–(CH₂)₆–NH₂ + n HOOC–(CH₂)₄–COOH → [–NH–(CH₂)₆–NH–CO–(CH₂)₄–CO–]ₙ + 2n H₂O
Uses: clothing, carpets, ropes and fishing nets, gears and bearings.
(With a dioyl chloride, ClOC–R–COCl, in place of the acid, HCl is eliminated instead of water.)

blocks.prompt: Q.6 Differentiate between the environmental degradation of poly(alkenes) and polyesters.
blocks.explanation: The difference comes from the backbone: polyesters have hydrolysable ester links, poly(alkenes) do not (26.5, 26.5.1).
